Hateful 8 is an enigma to me.

I find it almost infinitely rewatchable, but also find it to be mostly empty calories.

The atmosphere, the build up of tension, the chemistry between actors is all off the charts.

But what does the movie actually have to say?

I agree that for Tarantino to follow up a western set in the 1850's to a western set in the 1870's feels repetitive.

If you squint your eyes a bit, you can almost imagine Samuel L Jackson's character as an older Django.

Most of the same themes are repeated.

I also agree that everything after the twist feels more like an epilogue than a continuation of the story.

And I have *no idea* what the ending and the Lincoln letter have to do with each other.

This just fits into such a weird place in T's filmography, and even though I don't quite understand what I'm watching, I know I like it.

For what that's worth.

Once I finally did, I loved it.

yeah I can't remember the exact chapters but the flashback when Jodys gang arrive to the haberdashery really breaks the pace of the movie. until this point it comes in a really cool crescendo.

also the whole narrator thing. I can't decide if I like or dislike it but I don't think its necessary. I think it sort of broke the immersion. TH8 is very dialogue intensive like a theatre play. I guess it would have been better to just show who poisoned the coffee and keep the audience guessing if the person who did it was working alone or not.

despite the above I also think its one of tarantinos best works. the dialogue intensive style really ramps up the rewatch ability factor. I have seen it more times than pulp fiction and reservoir dogs combined .

I think it's Tarantino's strongest post-Kill Bill film, personally. I think Kill Bill ushered in an era of zaniness in Tarantino movies, and while it worked well in Kill Bill, it made all the other films seem messy to me, as much as I enjoyed Inglourious Basterds, that is my biggest criticism.

To me, while I still think The Hateful Eight could still use an edit, it felt a bit like Tarantino going back to what he did best - long scenes of tension through dialogue, with a fragmented narrative timeline witholding important context until it was necessary. It's got considerably less of the wackiness that you see in Kill Bill, Death Proof (to a lesser extent), IB and Django, and is better for it.

I'd probably rank it amongst my favourite Tarantino films, honestly.

I’ve recently watched it for the 3^rd time, and what I’ve concluded is that it hasn’t got any better or worse in the past 7 years. It’s a very entertaining but imperfect movie that is a little too long. 

Jackson’s big monologue is one of the finest things I’ve seen on film: it’s so infantile, so offensive, and so funny still. 

I remember it was hyped for its production qualities, whatever film stock or camera or whatever they chose to use, and just like with Dunkirk, it doesn’t make the least bit of difference to me. I don’t care if a movie is shot on an iPhone or million-dollar equipment. 

An interesting fact is that the guitar Russell smashes was an antique, on loan from a museum, and he wasn’t supposed to do that, obviously. So Leigh’s bewilderment is quite genuine in that scene.

I mean they even have Ennio Morricone using tracks from The Thing in Hateful 8 while also creating a new score. He has said the biggest inspirations for the film were The Thing and Reservoir Dogs

Its a good movie on his own. But its also Tarantinos most tarantinoesk Tarantino-movie.   
It covers a lot of ground, writing style, narrative technics and so on that he had done before. He assembled many of his favorite actors again for it. It has Morricone music, one of his favorite composers (where he also had used music from him before). He had also similar themes before, plus, as basically a variation of "The Thing", it has also his trademark of adapting and reconstructing his favorite movies in a different way. one of the standout things is IMO Daisy Dommergues character, other than that we are knee deep in Tarantinoland here. 

"Once upon a time in Hollywood" is also controversial, especially because of his offbeat and slow feeling early on, but for me it felt after Hateful 8 he was ready to close the past and try out some new things.

I see comments like this a lot and I’ve never understood the need for a film to “say” anything. A lot of replies on here that attempt to offer some meaning are very surface level anyways so what’s the point? Would that we could have more “empty calorie” movies of this caliber.

I had gotten tired of Tarantino's schtick with "Kill Bill" and he never really won me back over.   But being a lifelong Kurt Russell fanatic since first seeing the Escape movies as a kid, and with Walton Goggins having just wrapped up what is, in my opinion, the greatest villain performance of small or big screen of all time as Boyd Crowder in "Justified", not to mention the legendary Ennio Morricone helming the score, I went into this movie with high hopes. 

They were thoroughly disappointed.  It was overlong, and, as to be expected with QT, obnoxiously edgy and not half as clever as it thought it was.

It played like a 3 hour western reimagining of Reservoir Dogs without a fraction of the humor or suspense and absolutely zero sense of pacing.   It really felt like QT was trying to repackage his usual bag of grindhouse tricks in an arthouse dressing, as though it was his bid to be seen as a "serious" filmmaker.  But the end result was just a muddled mess of conflicting styles without even a single compelling narrative thread or character study to anchor it.  Just 3 hours of "watch all these horrible people gradually kill each other. "

Instead it was a slowish burn where everyone is trapped in a cabin for a little bit and one person has a secret and one other person is not who they seem and there is one twist and you know exactly what is going to happen. I felt like it needed to just lean into its premise a little harder.

Saw it in theater on release and not since.  I think my hindsight view of it is probably not as positive as it deserves.  I enjoyed it throughout, but what I enjoyed most was that building tension.  The whodunnit aspect was an engaging hook, but it doesn't pay off in a satisfying way, and as a result that wonderfully built tension just kind of deflates and left me somewhat disappointed.  I suspect if I rewatched it now, I'd be able to appreciate it more with the context, and with more of a focus on Tarantino's generally impressive craftsmanship, but I don't think it would come out near the top of his catalogue for me.

I unabashedly love this movie. It is a blast, and I have watched the extended cut multiple times. It’s my favorite winter movie.

Another commenter said it’s mostly empty calories. That’s probably not far off. The thing is, it’s a guilty pleasure. I can eat my veggies and watch a Kubrick or Bergman on workdays, but Friday night it’s Hateful Eight and a pizza.

Tarantino has talked about "hang out" movies a lot and it's a core part of his style. It's not a mistake or a misstep on his part. It's a consistent, intentional aspect of his filmmaking.

I happen to find it tiring. I'm glad he's found his audience though. He's definitely a genius.

I always thought the themes were pretty explicit. The movie was written during the initial Trump campaign, so much political polarization abound. Minnie’s Haberdashery serves as an analogy for the US, populated by a diverse, ideological cast of characters who all butt heads incessantly.

My take on the ending is Tarantino pleading for every “team” to come together, recognize each other’s humanity, and take out their rage on the real culprit for America’s woes: the ruling class that defrauded them all in the first place. Living together-but-separate is fatal, and learning to understand one another is the only key to survival.

Tends to happen a lot with Tarantino movies. It’s like he doesn’t know how to end them so he just says “fuck it” and has everyone start shooting each other. It worked great in *Reservoir Dogs* but not so much in anything that came after.

Its my personal favorite of his and I think its genius and possibly my favorite film of all time, in general. And tragically people tend to miss the message of the movie. The Civil War NEVER ended in America. Not in 1870 when this movie takes place and not now. A cultural wound split open during that time and it never fully healed. We have times when it looks like its going to heal and begin to scar over, and then something new happens—angry actions from extremist groups and politicians, confederate flag wavers still wishing they could secede, all those wrathful anti-Federal government talking points that are never about actual valid policy critiques and are merely civil war “States Rights” arguments meant to allow more far right wing social policies to be implimented without interference, etc.

We are still a hateful, angry, divided nation and nobody can agree on what America is. And we have fake liberals like John Ruth who dresses suave and Lincoln-esque beneath his caveman fur coat, but his behavior is clearly that of another racist caveman the moment he’s angered about something.

And the Jody Domingre gang represent a greater threat that requires a confederate marauder (Chris Mannix) and an anti-white Union soldier (Major Marquis) to work together for The Greater Good. So until there is a threat that threatens all Americans, it is highly unlikely that the hatred and grudges and rivalries that exist between various groups in America will be stitched together and become One people. 

10/10 film that gets better every time you watch it. I highly recommend The Extended Edition on Netflix!! 👌
